title: 2026/09/17 - PP (Part 1)
machineSummary: Commerce Commission officials said high 2024 energy prices and multinational strategies drove closures like Heinz Wattie's and McCain's. Debates focused on legislative options to block anti-competitive asset stripping, Carter Holt Harvey's regional exit, and supermarket duopoly power squeezing growers' margins through home brands.

chunks.text: Discuss the closure of Heinz Wattie's, Greeks and McCain's food processing. So, raise your hands to start with. Expect probably a little bit of a summary of what's happened, and there's going to be a lot of questions, I assume. Yeah. Thank you very much.

So yeah, very nice to be here this morning. I'm the small chair of the commission, Suzanne Stu, our Chief Executive. Good morning. And Andy Burgess, who's our GM of the infrastructure branch. It's lovely to be with so many farmers. I'll try and avoid talking about weather and tractors and such, and focus on Heinz Wattie and product processing facilities. So I think that we probably should start by saying we don't have particular insight into either of these ones that you're interested in, but we can talk about factors that

make life difficult for firms like that. And I think we can talk about domestic factors, but also I think it would be relevant to look into the ownership structure, and what was going on in the corporate entities prior to those decisions that were made. And on that point, I think we're all aware that multinational organizations have a kind of global portfolio allocation process, that depending on their capital structure, they may

choose to engage in things that are profitable from a tax point of view, like management fees and so on out of a country and licensing of brands and debt levels and so on. So, I don't know, I don't have any particular insight into what financial stress these processes were under at the time they made these decisions. But I do think it's probably relevant to those decisions.

To the other factors that have been raised, one that's related to the costs of energy, and another that's potentially related to the operation of the grocery sector. So we can answer questions about those, and help you think through both those matters.

Just on the grocery side of things, just which I think is, I'm not sure there's a lot to be discovered from there. I am aware that there was a category review process that affected Heinz Wattie, prior to the introduction of the Grocery Industry Competition Act.

So about the time when the Commerce Commission was doing its market study into groceries, there was a category review process, which is a common thing in supermarkets, and sometimes that leads to products being delisted. In fact, that's kind of part of the purpose of category reviews is to decide which products remain on the shelves and at what cost to the supermarkets.

So, that event, as my understanding is with Heinz Wattie, that event happened about four years before they closed. So it may have been a factor, but it wasn't the immediate stressor. If it was a factor, it was something that from which the effects built up over time.

On the energy side, it's no secret that wholesale energy prices were really, really high in 2024, as a result of a combination of factors, and that a number of processing operations, not just food, but also forestry processors and so on, really struggled and indeed closed during that period as a result, with high energy prices being pointed to as a contributing factor.

So I think you probably can't rule that out as a factor. And I suppose more than happy to talk about what's been and being done in that sector more recently to try and moderate those prices and get things on a much stronger track, as with energy, any kind of large non-tradable sector in New Zealand, industry reform and change is a slow

process and difficult one. But with clear direction and determination, better things can happen, and the commission's very much involved in those efforts. So I might just stop there, if that's all right. Yeah. Mr. Chair, and I'm going to take questions. Yes. We'll go straight to Steve Abel.

Thank you, Mr. Chair. Thank you very much for coming in. I wonder, we've got a very strong submission from a number of impacted parties, but one of the acknowledges from Heretonga Hostings near is the sort of system impact of losing processing capability as it affects growers and that local Hawkes Bay economy.

And everyone trying to work out what are reasonable interventions that any government should consider to protect that processing capability and recognize it as strategic significance-... for the whole economy and for food resilience. Notwithstanding the right of companies to sell up, are there options that you consider are reasonable to stop potentially anti-competitive behavior?

There's suggestions that the asset stripping of facility before it was ever put on the market as a going concern may have undermined the ability of a growers' cooperative to make a successful bid on taking over the facility. Mm. And what could any given government do to ensure that there's some period of time within which when a strategically significant facility such as McCain's or Heinz Beanz is going to close, that there's an option for local buyers or buyers from anywhere, to be honest, to have a
crack at taking it over as a going concern. Yeah, a really interesting set of issues in there. And I think what you're pointing to is the value of optionality. I certainly endorse that.

And as to whatever the owners did with the internal plant, that's a really interesting question. I don't know the facts of the matter. But I have seen in previous lives when I was working in private practice, I've seen situations where companies would rather take grinders to their stainless steel than- Yes... than leave the plant fall into a competitor's hands.

So they're deliberately trying to destroy capacity, take it out of the economy and specifically for, well, they would say for pro-competitive reasons, but of course pro-competitive being the thing that they And there's certainly some evidence that that's what happened in the case of McCain. Right. So that kind of conduct is, as I say, I have seen that personally before in a previous life, and it's always struck me as being something that's pretty destructive and all being in one company's interests, maybe not in the interests of competition and the

wider economy. So I think that's a policy issue, really. There's no regulatory tool, I don't think, that we could use to get at it. Potentially if there was a case under the Commerce Act under Section 36 or something like that, we may be able to take action, but those things are slow processes, and by the time you get started, everything's all in bits.

And so it's kind of too late. It's not really- A good follow on, really. Quick sup. Yeah. Just a quick sup. Do you know if there's examples abroad where there are legislative requirements, for example, for there to be some time period within which a business that's going to be closed or sold is available before such asset stripping can occur?

That seems to be an obvious thing that could happen as a- Yeah, I'm not aware of that, but we could do a bit of looking into that. Thank you. Yeah. I had a sup as well, which is nearly identical issue, but different industry. So I think this is wider than just what's happened in Hawke's Bay, and just your comment about it being a policy issue, yeah, it would be interesting to know what sort of legislative options we could be looking at.

The case of Carter Holt Harvey in the Nelson region closing up, even though it was profitable and there being four interested buyers in the plant, but two of which were genuine capable buyers. And on top of that, a situation where the region has significant windthrow of timber that needs to be processed following the 2024 floods. So there's a need to process the timber at a profitable plant, but decision made by the company to consolidate in the North Island and not sell the plant. So a loss of over 100 jobs, and then the

timber being shipped rather than being processed in the region. So, strategically, really problematic, really anti-competitive. We're seeing this across multiple parts of the manufacturing sector. So I would just be really keen to know what policy and legislative options you would think MPs could be looking at.

Because the issue came up when that happened around Section 36, but again, too slow. By the time you've gone through that process- Yeah, it's a very slow process everything's been sold up and scrapped, so. Yeah. So that's another interesting example. The one I was thinking of occurred in the dairy processing sector.

So I think as you're pointing out, these are issues that arise from time to time in a number of different industrial sectors. Probably is worth our while as a country thinking about how to react to them. I would just caution, though, that in some cases, we do end up with excess capacity, and it's not a bad...

So you wouldn't want the default to be always you've got to preserve the capacity. And I'm thinking here of, for example, meat processing- Yeah As a result of all us people out there milking cows, the flow of product through the meat works has dropped off a lot and there's a whole lot of stranded capacity.

And there's a question about how you rationalize that capacity when it's owned by a whole lot of different people. And while it's all there, it's highly competitive but potentially a bit inefficient. So look, I'm afraid I don't have an actual answer, but I do recognize the question that you're asking. I think it kind of goes both ways.

Yeah, because it just comes back to, doesn't it, when there's actually genuine competitive need. Yes. Yeah. So, Suze, you looked this up. So I'm just wondering, is there any mechanism available to protect sort of strategic assets in that respect? In this case, the farmers clearly rallied themselves pretty quickly and showed an intention to be able to move forward and then they were sort of hamstrung. But is there anything available to them or to us to allow a strategic asset like that to be protected or to give them the opportunity to-

They actually put in a bid. Yeah, to put in. Yeah. No, but yeah. Because it was... Yeah. Is there a pathway to do that? Not to my knowledge, short of getting a court injunction, but you'd need to have a rationale for how this was going to play out in court more than anything.

So if you've got bad actors on the other side, there's really nothing you can do about it? It's pretty tough. Look, and I'll tell you what, we do see this in a merger context as well. We see similar kinds of commercial strategic game playing, game playing in the formal sense, as regards who knows what and when things are happening. You see this play out in a number of different sectors quite recently in merger cases we've had this year.

But the short answer is no, and I'm not sure how you'd even get to that short of having a list of things that there were special requirements over or something of that sort, but I don't know if- Because reading the submission, some of the things that they proposed I don't think are necessarily viable. Like saying that they're competing with countries that can produce cheaper and what have you, and suggesting proposing tariffs which is not going to happen, I don't think. But this thing, this was one lever they had to

pull which just seemed really unfair that the carpet got ripped out. Yeah. Yeah. But there's not really anything that you can do about it. No, and as I said, in a merger context we've seen situations where there are credible bidders and they really struggle to get an opportunity. And it does go to strategic commercial conduct on the part of the people who currently own the assets.

Now, in response to your question earlier, has this been addressed anywhere around the world? Not to my knowledge, but I'm more than happy to have a look at that and see if we can throw you some advice on it. We'll go to Mark Cameron, who's online.

Good morning, everyone. Nice to see you all. I think the real question what we're asking to you good people, is what is the role of government, really? We appreciate, I just heard you mention court injunction. That's an interesting dynamic in so much that would be quite significant interference by the judiciary. So I think the ultimate question is, what is the role of government when strategic assets, for whatever reasons, either economically fail or by virtue of free market decide, to Rachel's point, to condense or solidify in

strategic regions of the country based on market tensions. So where do you think the role of the Crown ultimately lands? So you're really asking me a policy question on that one . I know. And I see you smiling, but really and truly, this is where it lands.
It's a fair question, and I wouldn't be doing this job if I didn't think that regulators could add value. I do think we can. And

also we do take that kind of view on some things, for example, cement recently. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. But that's kind of an ad hoc response to a particular situation, and I suppose what I would advocate would be something of if we think this is an issue, that something a little systematic that could be thought through in advance and you go, "Oh, well, what are the sorts of situations in which we want..." Our job is to promote competition, so all of this is the same direction that you folk are all going in here.

You're wanting to preserve the opportunity for more competition by using existing assets that we've already got. So fully endorse that as an objective. The mechanism is the hard part, and so I don't disagree. No, I appreciate that. I know it was a fickle question, but that I say that, and I'm glad that you offered spoke the way you did. We appreciate it's our role to do this. But at what point does the Crown interfere in private enterprise is the real question.

Mm-hmm. Yeah. Yes. Very good. Thank you Have you done any work on the margins that the growers get versus what the products are sold for? I mean, um- Oh, no, not specifically. We, no- It's a submission, isn't it? Right. We, we, we currently got before us a merger of, um, vegetable wholesalers.

Mm. Um, and, and we're working through that quite 'cause it's quite, quite a tricky, uh, matter actually 'cause the whole lot of huge variety and, and it, and, and competitive conditions are different in different parts of the country, so that's a difficult matter. But we're, we're, we're attacking that from a, um, sort of more principles, um, competitive basis by looking at conditions in each part of the country. We have not done that, that work, no.

Yeah. Well, it's, it's interesting. I mean, a loaf of bread is about $4.50 at the moment. Probably about 4 or 500 grams of flour in it. The gr- the, the grower gets 40 cents a kilogram for wheat, near enough. So, 20 cents of that $4.50 goes to the grower.

Mm. It's, it's, um, really interesting to see 'cause in Canterbury there's a lot of growers up in sticks changing land use. That's right. Yeah. They cannot make it work. Mm-hmm. No. And yet, um, they point to the fact that the product that's been made is, um, what?

200 times or whatever. Yeah. Mm. No, and, and I mean, as a, as a farmer, you're sort of painfully aware of the difference between gate prices and retail prices. Um, it, it's massive and, and that's why I think, you know, the, the out- out task and, and the one that you're focusing on here, which is promoting competition in the processing layer, um, is super important because the more competitive...

We see this in the meat industry now. It's more competitive because there's more capacity and more f- more individual players, um, and so therefore gate prices are higher. It's really, really obvious, and you can see it in, in the US in particular where meat- 100%... packaging is very concentrated. Mm. 'Cause it seems to me that there's a tension between that, uh, competitive principle to drive down consumer value and the farmer being sort of paradoxically the, the one that gets the worst return even though they're

the most essential to the product existing. And, and the, the question that seems to come from certainly growers recently that I've talked to is the, the question of what the markups are- Yeah... at the retail level. Whether they're reasonable. Transparency around what they're being told.

Yep. Um, so and so down the road has sold their head of broccoli for, versus what, you know, what, what they think it should be reasonably worth given what it's retailing for in that week. So- And so that kind of transparency on the, um, those who have the price brokering power because of their scale, i.e.

the supermarkets- Yeah. Mm... um, versus, uh, you know, the grower just has to take what they're offered really. Yeah. So there's a, there's an emerging, um, uh, area of antitrust law that looks at that, and that's like- Yeah... B2B transactions. Um, New Zealand's, you know, got a little way to go to get up to an international frontier in there, but we're, we're sort of working on that.

Uh, I'd say one other thing, though, um, a bit more generally about this, you know, you kind of characterize w- we want, we want strong competition right throughout the sector so the consumer gets the lowest price and there's an element of truth in that, but it's not, it's not entirely abs- absolutely accurate. You look at the way we looked at the North South Foodstuffs merger.

Our, our big concern there, uh, one of our big concerns there was that this was gonna be a three to two merger in the acquisition of groceries, so it was gonna, it was gonna concentrate the purchasing sector, uh, which was be to the detriment of the food suppliers. Mm.

Who would include growers and, and, and, and other manufacturers like Heinz, Motty and, and, and the like. So we see that, we, we see that balancing of market power as, um, as important for competition. Mm. Um, it's not always necessarily the lowest price. Um, it's you need, you need balanced competition, right?

No- nobody wants to watch me being thrashed at tennis by, um, Serena Williams. It's not, not competition. It's, it's a kind of... So that balancing of market power we think is quite important. Yeah. Interesting. So- Oh, I'll just say the other implication, which is not really relevant, but is the, the impact it has on the actual model of farming because some people use those, growing those legumes to sort of help, it fixes nitrogen or whatever-... so they don't need to use as much fertilizer.

So like it's part of the- Mm... part of the rotational planning for their farms. Absolutely. So if you suddenly have to change to another crop or do something different, it can have an impact- Well, they're just gonna switch to seed and bean... on the environment and on your farming model. Yeah. Or use more urea. Yeah. And they can re- grow grass in between or whatever. Yeah. Yeah. So it's- No, I totally get you... it has a trickle-down effect. It does. It really does. Yeah.

It, it... Right across the ecosystem and the way you started off with the, with the, you know, the, the workers and growers and around Hawitonga, you know, that's, that's a big impact there. Mm. Huge. Yeah, so that's where you sort of need to, I guess as a any subsequent government needs to get into that space of looking at the bigger picture and working out what's an appropriate intervention There's the consequences down the track, and it's very hard to bring it back once you've lost the facility.

Yeah, and it needs to be done in a forward-looking, principled kind of way, recognizing it could go either way in particular circumstances. Yeah. Well, it just did seem unconscionable in this situation that it was that the growers motivated themselves really quickly. They worked out that, did a study of the model, thought that it was sort of top-heavy and that they could reduce some costs and make it more efficient- Mm-hmm... in terms of the freezer space, in particular. There were all sorts of things that they'd done, the

research, and then it just got ripped out from under them. Mm-hmm. So, maybe another question I've got is around the home brand stuff, where- Oh, yeah... you've got the pressure to provide home brand from the suppliers. Mm-hmm. And then their branded product, which is on the same shelves.

Yeah. Mm-hmm. And, in discussion with different suppliers, that's basically saying that they're subsidizing their own product- Mm... because they're forced to sell the home brand stuff's basically under- Mm... cost of production. Mm-hmm. And that's just to get shelf space.

So if you don't supply it, you won't have shelf space. So have you done any research into that model? This is a fairly big issue in the grocery sector. And I'm sure you understand how the major retailers do this. Yeah. They put out tenders for the lowest price you can give me to supply me with a product that looks like this, and then that becomes my own brand.

In the process, I've learned about how much it costs to produce that. So when somebody comes along with a branded product that looks much the same, I already know quite a lot about your cost structure. That helps me in my negotiations. And then I get to choose where those sit on the shelf and at what price points.

So we recognize it's an issue. We recognize that it squeezes growers and producers. We don't have an answer for it yet. Yeah. Just to follow up on that is, is there something wrong with the system, do you think, where you can sell products as your own when you don't grow them, manufacture them, you're just selling them?

So you think because they've got so much power- Mm... the supermarkets can demand that a home brand type product be sold. I know the consumers like it because it's cheaper, but at the end of the day, it's squeezing growers out. Yeah. I think I'd just go back to the point that we really want more retail competition for groceries.

I speak for that as well, Steve. You got three parties happening to be at the table now and not Mark, but that have all proposed some sort of intervention in the supermarkets of different kinds, like anti-competitive or breaking up the duopoly in different ways. Do you think we're at a stage now with the challenges around the cost of food, but also potentially, the way the dominance and the power of the retailer in terms of the supermarkets, that it is appropriate for us to have those sorts of interventions?

Yeah, I can't obviously comment on these specific policies. No. Can't ask him for a political answer. I'm trying to not ask for a political answer. I'm trying to ask for a general principle of- I think it's-... are we at a stage where it's, we're in the right track to be looking at that? The commission's on record, as you know, for several years now, as saying that we think that the structure of the grocery retailing sector needs to be improved.

Yeah. And we've got a set of tools that are kind of behavioral regulation tools that were given to us a few years ago that we're using to try and push that. Mm-hmm. And so that's one way we can carry on down that road. We know that, and we've said this publicly, that it's a long, slow road. Mm-hmm.

And I know it annoys the supermarkets and imposes costs on them and so on. That's the current policy. And it will, I think it would actually improve com- there are some signs that it has sort of worked. Some people have used the wholesale regime to get a bit of scale and then go direct and now they're retailing in competition with Pack and Save nationwide.

There's Paddock to Pantry is doing that on a delivery basis. So that kind of process can work- Mm-hmm... but it's a pretty long, slow process. And ultimately, the aim is to change the structure, by which I mean there's more retailers- Yeah... more diverse retailers. Thank you very much. We've come to time.
Lovely. Appreciate you coming in this morning. Thank you. Thank you. That's great. Thank you.
